opening.headline: We explain why requests are concentrated in only one place despite launching multiple model servers using inference pools and inference gateways, and distinguish the impact of cluster version and API support discontinuation on AI workloads.
body: I have spun up four model server pods, but only one pod has a long queue, and the rest are idle. A typical load balancer counts the requests and divides them evenly, but the cost of one request varies greatly depending on the prompt length and cache state. In addition to this issue, AI service operators also encounter issues where deployment files that use older API versions are rejected after upgrading a cluster.

In this lesson, we first explain how one LLM request is processed on the GPU, KV cache, and batching. Next, we first check how the Gateway API Inference Extension selects requests by looking at the model server's status indicators and the roles of the InferencePool and Endpoint Picker. Next, we distinguish between the layers of the llm-d router, KServe, and Kubeflow, and examine the purpose and release schedule of the Kubernetes AI Conformance Program, and the impact of API deprecation on AI workloads.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Describe the impact of LLM request prompting, token generation, KV cache, and batching on server queuing and memory.
Can explain the purpose of the inference pool, inference gateway, and Kubernetes AI conformance program
Distinguish between release schedules and the impact of API deprecation on your AI workloads

screens.title: I increased the model server, but requests are concentrated in only one location.
screens.lead: Select the pods in the picture one by one to check the status of each server and why it is receiving a lot of requests.

visual.alt: The illustration shows a typical load balancer splitting requests evenly across four pods, but only one pod has a long queue.
labels: Generic load balancer (only counts requests and distributes evenly)

items.prompt: Pod 1: Queue is long and cache is full
items.answer: This pod is processing long prompts, which results in queued requests piling up and KV cache usage nearing its limit. The KV cache is a space in the GPU memory where the intermediate calculation results of tokens already processed by the server are stored. This is covered in more detail in the third screen of this lesson. Even if a new request comes in, processing cannot start and you have to wait. Continuing to send requests to this pod is the crux of the problem.

The remaining pods have little wait time and some cache headroom, but the load balancer doesn't know about this. Even though the number of servers has been increased, the delay remains the same for users.

items.prompt: A typical load balancer only counts requests.
items.answer: A typical load balancer treats each request as a job of equal size and divides it evenly among the servers. However, it cannot distinguish between servers that are processing long prompts and servers that are idle. LLM requests vary greatly in cost, so equalization of the number of requests does not equal equalization of load.

items.prompt: Another question: How do cluster versions and standards match?
items.answer: To run the model server reliably, you must also manage the cluster version. Deployments can break when a version reaches end-of-support or an old API is removed. We cover release schedules and API deprecations later in the class.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the problem looks like, let's think about a similar experience.

screens.title: Recall: the illusion of equal distribution.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: I launched several model servers, but requests are concentrated in only one. Have you ever seen a similar situation?
items.answer: If you have increased the number of servers but the delay has not decreased, it is likely that the problem is distribution. Comparing queue and cache usage across servers reveals uneven load.

items.prompt: Was round robin fair in systems where the cost of a single request varied greatly from one another?
items.answer: For regular web services with similar request sizes, round robin is fair. In LLM services where the request size is dozens of times different, the same number of times does not mean the same load.

items.prompt: Have you ever suddenly had your deployment files rejected after upgrading a cluster?
items.answer: Manifests that use an outdated apiVersion will be rejected in releases when that version is no longer available. AI workloads often rely on the latest features, making the timing of upgrades more critical.

screens.outro: First, let's look at the full picture of the inference gateway.

screens.title: How one LLM request is processed by the GPU
screens.lead: Select the right arrows to follow the sequence: prompt processing, token generation, KV cache, and batching. Knowing this process will help you understand why the load on each server varies even if the number of requests is the same.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the prompt processing section and token generation section of one request on the time axis, with the GPU memory divided into model weights and KV cache as bars below.
labels: Prompt processing (prefill): Calculate all input at once
Token generation (decode): tokens in order one by one
Memory Limit: Limit on the number of further requests you can receive

steps.title: 1. Process the prompt at once (prefill)
steps.body: When a request arrives, the server processes the entire input prompt first. Since all of the tokens in the prompt are already known, they can be calculated in parallel all at once, and this section makes good use of the GPU's parallel computing power. During this process, the first output token is created, and the key and value of each token are calculated together. The longer the prompt, the longer this section will be.

steps.title: 2. Generate tokens one by one (decode)
steps.body: From then on, the server sequentially creates output tokens, one at a time. The next token depends on the preceding token and cannot be parallelized. This section does not use up the GPU's computational power, tends to block memory access, and takes up most of the time for one request. The longer the output, the longer this section becomes.

steps.title: 3. KV cache takes up GPU memory
steps.body: Each time you create a token, you will need the key and value values from the previous token. To avoid recalculating each time, already calculated values ​​are stored in GPU memory, which is the KV cache. The longer the prompt and output, the larger the KV cache per request. One paper used the 13 billion parameter OPT model as an example and calculated that each token can use about 800KB, and a single request generating up to 2048 tokens can use up to about 1.6GB. The numbers vary depending on the model structure, so read this as an example to get a feel for the size.

steps.title: 4. Batching increases throughput and memory sets the limit.
steps.body: Processing requests one at a time wastes the GPU, so the server bundles multiple requests together and processes them together. Throughput increases because the model weights read once are shared among multiple requests. When a request is finished, it is removed from the batch and a new request comes in. However, the number of requests that can be bundled is limited by the memory occupied by the KV cache. In the same paper, in the example of loading a 13 billion parameter model on a 40GB GPU, model weights took up about 65% of the memory and the KV cache, which is the request state, took up about 30%. When the KV cache is full, new requests wait in the queue even if there is compute power remaining.

steps.title: 5. So the cost varies greatly from request to request
steps.body: Requests with long prompts have long processing intervals and take up a lot of KV cache, and requests with long outputs hold the cache for a long time. Even if the number of requests is the same, the queue length and KV cache utilization will vary significantly depending on which server receives the longer requests. Even if GPU compute utilization appears to be low, the memory may be full and no new requests can be accepted, so the health of the server should be viewed through indicators such as number of queued requests and KV cache utilization.

steps.title: 6. Prefix cache and LoRA adapter
steps.body: If multiple requests share the same prefix (such as a long system prompt or the same document), you can skip prompt processing for that portion by reusing the already computed KV cache. This is called prefix caching, and what is reduced is the prompt processing section and the token generation section is not reduced. LoRA is a fine-tuning method that additionally learns only a small, low-dimensional matrix while fixing the weights of the base model. In serving, adapters can be interchanged with one base model, and which adapters are available may vary from server to server. Whether the prefix cache is hit or not and whether or not the adapter is present are also factors in deciding whether to choose a server.

screens.outro: Now that we understand why request costs are not uniform, let's look at the structure of an inference gateway that looks at this state information and picks requests.

screens.title: Gateway API Inference Extension and Inference Gateway
screens.lead: Select a number marker in the picture to see a description of what the component does and what existing element it replaces.

visual.alt: Schematic diagram of how a client's request passes through the gateway and Endpoint Picker to the InferencePool's model server pod.
labels: KV cache utilization, queue length, active LoRA adapter

markers.label: Inference Gateway
markers.title: Extend your existing gateway for inference
markers.body: Gateway API Inference Extension optimizes and standardizes routing for generative models hosted directly on Kubernetes. This is a method of extending an existing gateway that supports Envoy's ext-proc and Gateway API into an inference gateway. It covers model-aware routing and LoRA models that route by looking at model names.

markers.label: Endpoint Picker
markers.title: Inference router to choose the best replica
markers.body: Endpoint Picker (EPP) is an implementation of an inference router. For each request, we look at the metrics and capabilities of the model server to determine the most appropriate endpoint in terms of cost and performance. The gateway forwards the request based on this selection.

markers.label: InferencePool
markers.title: Bundle of same model server pods
markers.body: An InferencePool is a group of Pods that use the same accelerator, the same base model, and the same model server. Although it has some overlap with Service, it does not obscure Service but is an abstraction tailored to the LLM model server bundle. HTTPRoute's backendRefs points to InferencePool instead of Service.

markers.label: server metrics
markers.title: Look at the status of the server, not the number of requests
markers.body: Model servers provide performance, availability, and feature information such as prefix cache status and LoRA adapter availability. Endpoint Picker tracks KV cache utilization, queue length, and active LoRA adapters for routing.

markers.label: Top AI Gateways
markers.title: Can be placed side by side with external model services
markers.body: When used with a higher-level AI gateway, you can put your self-hosted model alongside an external model service. Incremental rollouts based on serving priorities, for example separation of delay-sensitive chat and batch summaries, or traffic splitting are also supported.

screens.outro: Next, let's read the code to see how InferencePool is declared.

screens.title: Settings for InferencePool to select model server candidates
screens.lead: Below is an example of an InferencePool resource. Select a line range from the description on the right to read what each field does.

data.code:
apiVersion: inference.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: InferencePool
metadata:
  name: vllm-qwen3-32b
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: vllm-qwen3-32b
  targetPorts:
    - number: 8000
  endpointPickerRef:
    name: vllm-qwen3-32b-epp
    port:
      number: 9002
    failureMode: FailOpen

notes.note: Declare an InferencePool resource at inference.networking.k8s.io/v1. The name becomes an identifier pointing to the pool, and the HTTPRoute's backendRefs points to this pool instead of the Service.
The selector's label must exactly match the label attached to the model server pod. If there is no match, the pod will not be part of the pool and the candidate will be empty.
targetPorts are the ports that the gateway will route to the pods in the pool. This must be the same port on which the model server actually receives requests.

endpointPickerRef points to the Endpoint Picker service, which looks at key metrics from the model server and makes routing decisions. If failureMode is FailOpen, the EPP forwards requests to the endpoint picked by the gateway when the endpoint is choppy or unresponsive.

screens.outro: Next, we will distinguish where the implementation is located and what layer it is placed on.

screens.title: llm-d router with KServe and Kubeflow
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what each standard API, routing implementation, and serving platform is responsible for.

tabs.label: standard API
tabs.body: The Gateway API Inference Extension repository houses the lightweight EPP and InferencePool API and conformance testing. The lightweight EPP is the implementation provided for conformance testing and is where the standard is defined. Objects like InferenceObjective represent the priority level of a request by linking it to a pool.

tabs.label: Routing Implementation
tabs.body: The Endpoint Picker and related APIs will continue to be developed in the llm-d router repository. The standard API maintains the same appearance, and the actual evolution of the routing algorithm occurs in the implementation. To determine which EPPs your gateway implementation supports, check the documentation for that implementation.

tabs.label: serving platform
tabs.body: KServe is a CNCF project that serves models on Kubernetes, and Kubeflow is an ML workflow platform. They form the upper layer of model deployment and are used on top of or alongside routing standards. Inference pools and gateways solve the routing problem in front of the model servers they deploy.

tabs.label: Classification
tabs.body: API standards, routing implementations, and serving platforms are different layers. When a problem arises, you can reduce the number of things to check by distinguishing which layer the problem is from. If requests are concentrated in one direction, we look at the routing layer first, and if distribution or version is an issue, we look at the serving platform first.

screens.outro: Now that we've looked at routing, let's look at a common baseline across platforms: the AI Conformance Program.

screens.title: Kubernetes AI Conformance Program
screens.lead: Below is a checklist summarizing the requirements for an AI Conformance Program. Select the underlined passages to determine the intent of each item.

data.text:
Kubernetes AI Fit Checklist (Summary)  
Prerequisite: The platform first has basic Kubernetes conformance  
Target: Training, inference, and agentic workloads  
Requirement Item: Gateway API support for inference  
Requirement Item: Rescheduling  
Requirement Item: Accelerator node autoscaling  
Requirement Item: HPA Behavior of Accelerator Pods  
Deliverable: Checklists and links to public evidence and automated test results

marks.span: The platform first has basic Kubernetes conformance
marks.note: AI conformance is a program that builds on top of the basic Kubernetes conformance. Platforms that do not have basic suitability cannot apply.

Target workloads are training that requires accelerators and predictable scheduling, inference where latency, routing, and scaling are important, and agent-like workloads that interweave long-running tasks with tools and memory.
This topic links directly to the inference gateway for this class. This means that the platform must provide the necessary functionality for routing inference traffic.

This item states that nodes with accelerators such as GPUs must be able to increase or decrease depending on the load. When a pod with an increased number of replications becomes Pending due to lack of space, the node autoscaler adds an accelerator node and cleans up less used nodes.

marks.span: Checklists and links to public evidence and automated test results
marks.note: The certification application is a structured self-assessment that includes checklists, links to public evidence, and automated test results for review. The goal is to ensure that AI applications that run on one platform will also work on other platforms.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the release schedule covering cluster versions and API deprecations.

screens.title: Release schedule and API deprecation
screens.lead: Select the arrows to the right to see the sequence of release lifetimes, API removals, manifest migrations, and upgrades.

steps.title: 1. Life of minor versions
steps.body: Kubernetes continues to release patches for each minor version, then enters maintenance mode and reaches its end of life. The Releases page displays the latest patch releases and end-of-support dates for each minor version. Check this page for the end of support date for the minor version you are running to reflect it in your upgrade schedule.

steps.title: 2. Result of discontinued version
steps.body: Out-of-support releases do not receive security updates and bug fixes. You need to know the end-of-support date for the version of your cluster so you can work backwards to schedule your upgrade.

steps.title: 3. APIs being removed
steps.body: Beta API versions will no longer be available in a future release. Deprecated API migration guidance outlines which API versions have become deprecated by release and how to migrate. Already stored objects will continue to be accessible with the new API, but manifests using the old apiVersion will be rejected.

steps.title: 4. Previous example: HPA
steps.body: HorizontalPodAutoscaler's `autoscaling/v2beta2` is not available since v1.26, and `v2beta1` is not available since v1.25. It should be moved to `autoscaling/v2` and the fields will also change. `targetAverageUtilization` is replaced by `target.averageUtilization` and `target.type: Utilization`.

steps.title: 5. Upgrade order
steps.body: The kubeadm upgrade starts with control plane nodes and progresses to worker nodes. You can't skip minor versions, so you have to bump up one minor at a time. Even if you want to skip it, you'll have to go through an intermediate version, so the shorter the time until support ends, the tighter your plans will be.

screens.outro: Now, let's move on to the example and explain the process of solving the flood of requests using the inference pool.

screens.title: Explanation 1: Resolving requests concentrated in one place using inference pool
screens.lead: There is a normal Service in front of four model server pods, and only one pod is overloaded. Select the right arrow to follow the instructor's solution.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: There is a normal Service in front of the four vLLM model server pods, only one pod has a long queue and the rest are idle. Even if you add more servers, the same phenomenon repeats.

steps.title: Step 1: Find the cause in the request cost
steps.body: The Service divides requests evenly among the Pods, but the costs of the requests are not equal. Depending on the length of the prompt and the state of the KV cache, one request may take much longer than another. The cause is not the number of requests, but an imbalance in request costs.

steps.title: Step 2: Bind Pods to InferencePool
steps.body: Group pods that use the same model and the same accelerator into an InferencePool, and ensure that the selector exactly matches the pod label. Change HTTPRoute's backendRefs to point to InferencePool instead of Service.

steps.title: Step 3: Let the Endpoint Picker select the candidates
steps.body: When you connect an EPP with an endpointPickerRef, the EPP looks at each pod's KV cache utilization, queue length, and active LoRA adapters and chooses the best replica. Requests flow to idle pods, so the load varies evenly. The behavior when the EPP does not respond is determined by failureMode.

steps.title: Step 4: Divide your priorities
steps.body: Delay-sensitive chat and batch summaries are handled in the same pool, but at different priority levels. Objects like InferenceObjective associate the priority of a request with the pool.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: We needed a router that looked at the status of the server rather than the number of requests, and the unit that reads that status was the InferencePool. A complete design requires determining what happens when the router breaks down.

screens.outro: Next, I will explain a situation where deployment is broken due to an API removed during an upgrade.

screens.title: Commentary 2: When deployment breaks due to API removed by upgrade
screens.lead: After uploading the cluster, the manifest using an old apiVersion is rejected. Select the right arrow to follow the inspection sequence.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: After bringing up a cluster, the model server's HPA manifest is rejected. The manifest uses `autoscaling/v2beta2`. Rejection is expected, as that version has been deprecated since v1.26.

steps.title: Step 1: Check the list of removed APIs
steps.body: Before upgrading, first check the release notes and deprecated API migration guidance for a list of APIs that will be removed in this upgrade period. Proactive confirmation is much faster than finding the cause after the fact.

steps.title: Step 2: Find uses in your repository
steps.body: Search the repository's manifest and charts to find any places that use the removed version. Model server deployment is often managed by multiple teams, so fixing just one location is not enough.

steps.title: Step 3: Switch to the new API and reflect fields
steps.body: Change the field to `autoscaling/v2` to reflect the field change. Replace `targetAverageUtilization` with `target.averageUtilization` and `target.type: Utilization`. If you just change the name, an error will occur in verification.

steps.title: Step 4: Upload and confirm one miner at a time
steps.body: kubeadm upgrades cannot skip minor versions, so they are incremented by one level. Ensure AI compliance items are maintained after each step, namely inference gateway and accelerator autoscaling.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Release lifetime and API removal are direct inputs into upgrade planning. It's important for the Model Servicing team to be aware of the cluster team's release schedule so they can proactively fix deployments that depend on APIs scheduled for removal.

screens.outro: Let me summarize the key points by combining the two cases.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Standards that align with stateful routing
screens.lead: We will organize what we have seen so far into one standard.

paragraphs: An LLM request consists of a section that processes the prompt at once and a section that creates tokens one by one, and the intermediate results of the processed tokens are stored in GPU memory as a KV cache. This memory determines the number of requests the server can receive simultaneously, so even if the number of requests is the same, the load on the server varies.

An inference gateway is a model-aware router that picks requests by looking at health metrics from model servers. An InferencePool is a collection of server pods of the same model, and the Endpoint Picker looks at KV cache utilization, queue length, and active LoRA adapters to select the appropriate replica.

The standard API, routing implementation, and serving platform are different layers. The Gateway API Inference Extension takes on the standards, the llm-d router takes on the evolution of the implementation, and KServe and Kubeflow take on the upper layers of model deployment.

The AI Conformance Program establishes common standards for aligning the behavior of AI workloads across platforms. Release lifespan and API removal directly affect your upgrade plans, so you should regularly check end-of-support dates and APIs scheduled for removal.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: LLM requests have different costs and must be distributed based on the state of the server rather than the number of requests. Cluster versions are governed by end-of-support dates and removed APIs.

screens.lead: Each row of the table is a problem addressed in this lesson. Read on to find out which tier the symptom is and where to check first.

data.notes: If you first classify the class in which symptoms appear, the scope for confirmation is greatly reduced. Routing looks at server health metrics, Upgrades looks at release schedules and API versions.

glossary.def: This is a Gateway API Inference Extension resource that represents a group of pods that use the same model server.
It is an implementation of an inference router that looks at the metrics of the model server and selects a replica to send the request to.
This is a routing implementation repository that develops the Endpoint Picker and related APIs.
It is a common standard that sets out the features that the Kubernetes platform must have to run AI workloads stably.
Older API versions, such as beta, will no longer be available in a future release. You need to move your manifest to the new version.

This is a space where the key and value of tokens already processed by the server are stored in GPU memory. The longer the request, the larger it becomes, limiting the number of requests that can be processed simultaneously.

misconceptions.myth: Even with a general load balancer, LLM traffic becomes equal.
misconceptions.fact: LLM requests have very different costs depending on prompt length and cache state, so evenly splitting the number of requests results in uneven load. You need a router that looks at the indicators of the model server and makes a selection.

misconceptions.myth: Cluster upgrades have no impact on workload.
misconceptions.fact: Manifests that write a removed API version will be rejected. Before upgrading, you should check which APIs are being removed and move their manifests.

misconceptions.myth: AI conformance certifies the quality of the model.
misconceptions.fact: AI suitability is a criterion for determining whether a platform has the ability to run AI workloads reliably and is not related to model quality.

misconceptions.myth: If GPU utilization is low, there is room on the server.
misconceptions.fact: The token generation section does not use up computational power, while the KV cache occupies memory. Even if compute utilization is low, if memory is full, no new requests will be received and the queue will be long.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The cost of an LLM request varies greatly depending on prompt length, output length, and KV cache occupancy.
The inference gateway picks requests by looking at server metrics.
InferencePool and Endpoint Picker are the key to candidate selection.
AI conformance is a common criterion across platforms.
Release lifetimes and API removals factor into your upgrade plans.

checks.q: Two servers are processing the same number of requests. Server A has long queues and full KV cache, but GPU compute utilization is low. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Server A has free space, so it can send more requests.
Server A is not accepting new requests because its memory is full due to long prompts or long output.
Server A's GPU computation is the bottleneck, so increasing the utilization rate solves the problem.
Since the number of requests is the same, the load on both servers is also the same.
checks.explain: Because the KV cache occupies GPU memory, limiting the number of requests that can be processed simultaneously, queues can be long even when compute utilization is low.

wrong.0: If memory is full, new requests will wait in the queue.
wrong.2: The bottleneck in this case is not compute power, but memory and queues.
wrong.3: The prompt and output length for each request are different, so the load can vary greatly for the same number of requests.
